newsitem.title: KENYA: Ethiopian, Somali forces exchange fire over border.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopian, Somali forces exchange fire over border.

text.p: Somali and Ethiopian forces exchanged artillery fire on Monday night after shells slammed into Ethiopian territory during heavy battles between Somali factions, residents were quoted as saying on Tuesday.
Fighting broke out late on Monday between Moslem fundamentalist Somali militiamen and the Somali National Front (SNF) movement, aid officials quoted residents of the Somali town of Dolow as saying.

"It was very heavy. It seems al-Ittihad came in and attacked the SNF in Dolow and Dr Ali Nuur, the deputy chairman of the SNF was killed along with two other SNF," a Western aid official told Reuters.

He said he had no reports of civilian casualties in Dolow, on both banks of a river marking the border. The city is divided into two halves -- one in Ethiopian territory and the other in Somali territory.
"The bridge linking Dolow-Somalia to Dolow-Ethiopia was destroyed on Monday night and shells went from Dolow-Somalia to Dolow-Ethiopia on the other side of the bridge," the official added.
"The Ethiopian army retaliated and shelled the hell out of Dolow-Somalia," said the official, adding most al-Ittihad forces in Dolow-Somalia had since pulled back to the town of Lugh to the south.

The official was speaking by telephone from northwestern Kenya, which borders both Ethiopia and western Somalia. There was no comment from the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa on the reports of Ethiopian involvement in fighting in western Somalia.

The Moslem fundamentalist al-Ittihad al-Islam movement said on Monday its militiamen repulsed Ethiopian troops that attacked one of its bases in Dolow on Sunday. But the aid official could not confirm Ethiopian forces were involved in the battle.

Ethiopia troops backed by helicopter gunships and artillery mounted a two-day incursion into the Gedo district of western Somalia last month in support of the SNF against al-Ittihad, blamed by Addis Ababa for recent bombings in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia said its raid was directed against fundamentalist bases and training camps and more than 200 people were killed.
Ethiopian officials said their forces might return for more attacks on what they called "terrorists" operating from Somalia.

Ahmed Bile, secretary of the al-Ittihad al-Islam group, told reporters in Mogadishu on Monday Ethiopian troops crossed into Somalia on Sunday and attacked Dolow, some 500 km (312 miles) southwest of Mogadishu.
Another al-Ittihad official, Hassan Dahir Awies, said the attackers were repulsed, three Ethiopian soldiers were killed, a number were wounded and some weapons were captured on Sunday.
Al-Ittihad said its forces killed at least 150 Ethiopian soldiers in last month's battles. The group said it also downed an Ethiopian helicopter and destroyed a tank.
The incursion prompted al-Ittihad to send reinforcements from Mogadishu to Gedo and its other bases in western Somalia.
"It was unwise of the Ethiopians to think they could go into western Somalia, hit al-Ittihad and pull out and the problem might go away. In fact it is getting bigger," said another aid official.
He said he had heard that Ethiopian forces were arming the SNF but al-Ittihad had captured large amounts of the weapons.
Somalia has had no central government and has been divided into various areas controlled by rival clan factions since the overthrow of late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991.
In 1977, Barre's government forces invaded Ethiopia and within three months had overrun the Ogaden region. But Ethiopia recaptured the Ogaden in 1978 in a Soviet and Cuban-led counterattack.
